claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a compositionally complex, single-phase solid solution with a uniform microstructure.
The initial alloy has high toughness and strong resistance to brittle fracture.
The initial alloy exhibits ductile crack propagation under standard quasi-static testing.
Extended high-temperature cyclic mechanical loading causes constituent elements to redistribute from grain interiors to grain boundaries.
The loading-induced elemental redistribution is diffusion-assisted.
The resulting grain-boundary enrichment can occur without rapid grain coarsening.
The resulting grain-boundary enrichment can occur without classic intermetallic precipitation or large intermetallic precipitates.
Subtle grain-boundary microsegregation lowers grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes crack nucleation and brittle intergranular fracture under service loads.
After prolonged cyclic thermomechanical exposure, the alloy will have lower fracture toughness than the as-cast control.
After exposure, the alloy will show an increased incidence of brittle intergranular fracture features relative to the as-cast control.
After exposure, grain boundaries will show subtle compositional inhomogeneity relative to the initial baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies principally during prolonged exposure near 0.7–0.8 of the melting temperature under cyclic mechanical stress.
Rapid loading or short exposure may provide insufficient time for diffusion-driven microsegregation.
Thermally activated diffusion and segregation are well-known phenomena.
Conventional-alloy toughness loss is directly associated with coarse or brittle grain-boundary precipitate formation.
